item.title: A Terminal Illness Sets a Cruel Deadline for the Estranged
item.description:
Family Dynamics

A Terminal Illness Sets a Cruel Deadline for the Estranged

The royal family’s divide reveals why a health crisis can reopen old wounds.

Posted July 22, 2026

Key points
  • A life-threatening diagnosis can trigger feelings of intense grief and guilt for estranged relatives.
  • With a deadline, the estranged ask: Should I call? Would my presence help? If I stay away, will I regret it?
  • lllness requires estranged relatives to understand that grief can exist, even when a reunion is impossible.
Source: UK Government / Crown Copyright

The recent reunion of King Charles with his son Prince Harry, Harry’s wife Meghan, and their children seemed to be a classic example of how illness can fuel reconciliation. After a previous brief meeting with Harry alone, Charles—a father battling cancer—reportedly moved forward in choosing contact over silence, bringing his son and grandchildren back into the family circle.

Illness raises the emotional stakes, compresses time, and can make compassion feel urgent. For loved ones as well as the patient, fighting a terminal disease may sharpen awareness of the sand slipping faster through the hourglass of life.

In Charles’s case, however, illness has not reunited all the parties involved. The estrangement arose six years ago, after Harry and Meghan rejected royal life to make a new home in California. His family considered the move a deeply hurtful betrayal; two years later, when Harry and Meghan returned to England for the funeral of his grandmother, Queen Elizabeth, the couple conspicuously did not even speak to his elder brother, Prince William, and William’s wife, Princess Kate.

Relations worsened drastically when Harry’s tell-all autobiography, Spare, shone a harsh light on his family, particularly William. The resulting acrimony continues to keep the brothers apart, despite Harry’s stated wish to reunite as well as Kate’s own struggle against cancer.

A deadline for estranged relationships

A life-threatening diagnosis often triggers complicated feelings for estranged relatives, including intense grief, guilt, and pressure for last-minute reconciliation. It may force the estranged to weigh their emotional safety against a desire for closure. The new urgency may resurrect issues the relatives have avoided for years.

The impending deadline prompts every relative to consider:

  • Should I call?
  • Would my presence help or harm?
  • If I stay away, will I regret it?
  • If I return, will I lose the boundaries that made life bearable?

Friends, extended family, neighbors, and clergy may urge reconciliation, with admonitions like “life is short” or “you’ll be sorry if you don’t go.” But outsiders rarely understand estrangement in its full complexity. A self-appointed “peacemaker” may try to force a bedside reunion that neither party has consented to.

True, avoidance may evolve into regret. But the estranged must consider whether it’s safe to reconcile. If the relationship was abusive, humiliating, or chronically destructive, it may be better to stay away.

The tension between mercy and self-protection is often the central emotional conflict for the estranged. A family member may feel grief, anger, pity, fear, tenderness, and dread—all within minutes.

Family systems theory adds another layer. A leading theorist, Murray Bowen, used the term “emotional cutoff” to describe how people manage intense family anxiety by distancing physically or emotionally. Bowen-oriented researchers have argued that while cutoff may reduce immediate distress, unresolved emotional attachment may remain beneath the surface.

Illness tests that arrangement. A diagnosis, a prognosis, even a hospital room can reactivate a whole system: old alliances, old grievances, old roles. The “responsible one” may be summoned to organize care. The “difficult one” may be blamed for staying away.

Bowen believed that the more a nuclear family maintains some level of viable emotional contact among its generations, the more orderly and less conflicted life’s processes will be for all involved.

“You have inherited a lifetime of tribulation,” Bowen said the day before he died. “Everybody has inherited it. Take it over. Make the most of it, and when you have to decide you know the right way, do the best you can with it.”

Other psychological challenges for the estranged

Here’s how a diagnosis can change an estranged family member’s perspective:

Anticipatory Grief and Regret: News of an impending death often revives buried pain. Many estranged individuals wrestle with the finality of not having resolved past conflicts. They fear they will eventually get stuck in “what-if” scenarios and feel profound regret.

Pressure to Reconcile: A terminal illness can spur sudden attempts at reconnecting; however, if the estrangement is rooted in past abuse, this can be risky. Reconnecting on a dying relative’s terms can cause more psychological harm than positive closure.

Navigating Boundaries: If the estranged decides to re-engage, professionals recommend setting and maintaining strict emotional limits. A safe way to address past trauma in a safe space might be to write a letter or have a difficult conversation that includes a mediator.

Caregiver Resentment: An estranged family member who suddenly appears on the scene may upset relatives who have already established day-to-day caregiving. This disruption may create more resentment than comfort.

Estate and Will Complications: Impending death frequently prompts sudden communication from long-absent relatives. They may be seeking information about inheritances, and that can lead to heightened tensions or legal battles over the estate.

Blogger Traci Foust didn’t weigh any such consequences when she decided to visit her dying sister after a 12-year estrangement. Foust wrote about seeing her sister one last time: skinny, jaundiced, her breathing ragged, the end clearly near.

“What ignorant cowards an unfixable past can make us,” she wrote in a moving essay titled “What I Said to My Estranged Sister on Her Deathbed.” “My sister was barely hanging ­ on . . . ‘Hold me,’ was the last thing she said . . . I curled the whole front of my body into hers, squeezing through her sickness, trying to get inside all those years we had wasted.”

But a serious health crisis does not affect everyone in the same way, as is obvious in the public example of William and Kate, and Harry and Meghan. Here, a potentially terminal disease was no magic bullet, dissolving history and hurts in favor of forgiveness. Rather, their father’s illness clarifies the brothers’ unfinished business of injury, loyalty, love and loss.

For some, that clarity becomes an opening. For others, it confirms the need for distance. Either way, illness requires estranged relatives to make hard decisions under the shadow of mortality—and to understand that grief can exist, even when a reunion is impossible.

item.title: What Explains a Person's Sense of Entitlement?
item.description:
Narcissism

What Explains a Person's Sense of Entitlement?

Former kings and queens behave differently from you and me.

Posted July 22, 2026

Key points
  • Entitlement may stem from "fabricated self-importance" resembling royal behavior.
  • Modern entitlement borrows from influencer culture, normalizing disregard for social etiquette.
  • Everyday entitlement is displayed in actions like ghosting, line-cutting, and treating others like servants.

Back in the 1990s, I sat with His Holiness the Dalai Lama; this meeting was highlighted by my studies on reincarnation in the parapsychology program at Duke University's Rhine Research Institute. I had learned that a psychiatrist at the University of Virginia, Ian Stevenson, spent more than 40 years investigating more than 2,500 cases of children who remembered their past lives, including details like their previous names and the causes of their deaths; in 11 cases, the children had birthmarks that supposedly resembled the fatal wounds of the person they claimed to have been. I found Stevenson's work fascinating. This is in addition to Sogyal Rinpoche’s explanation in “The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying” of why most people don’t consciously remember their past lives and belief in the transmigration of souls through sundry lifetimes.

As a psychotherapist for the past 17 years, I have observed a phenomenon that I labeled in a previous post as “fabricated self-importance.” While the Dalai Lama and children who remember past lives are the opposite of people who fabricate self-importance, the fabricators instead behave as if they are reincarnations of kings and queens from previous epochs. The latter appear on social media and behave like famous public figures—the behavior is conscious, intentional, performative, and strategic, as well as inauthentic and perhaps absurd. It is the deliberate performance of putative status superiority for transactional gain deployed by people who conduct their lives as if they’re always doing something extremely important. For example, they double-book lunches to see—à la Black Mirror—which of their “friends” will yield more power points.

I’ve recently noticed a sub-genre of this affliction that I hadn’t previously fully accounted for: an endemic sense of entitlement that seems to have trickled down from these people who are famous for being famous, namely influencers, into real life. “Ask for forgiveness, not for permission,” I heard one of them say. There may be an "outside the box" explanation for this disregard: The “Do you know who I am?” attitude. I am only half-joking when I suggest that these people must have been kings or queens in their past lives.

Here are 10 behaviors I have observed that have led me to this conclusion:

10. Texting at red lights, causing three to five cars behind them to miss the next green light. The idea that a DM would cause the woman behind them to miss her ultrasound doesn’t compute. Whatever they are doing is clearly the most important priority and cannot wait.

9. Correcting a waiter’s pronunciation of a foreign wine, delivered like someone who once had vintners hanged them for lesser offenses.

8. Taking a video call on speakerphone in a waiting room or on a train, converting a public space into your private office. The royals feel that allowing common people to overhear their intimate dealings will inspire them to want to be great.

7. Cutting the line at a coffee shop under the guise of “just asking a quick question,” which somehow becomes an order. Customizing latte orders is an artistic expression of uniqueness. We must let these anointed artists beautify our world in their uniqueness each morning.

6. Ghosting “the help,” closure is a courtesy the royals do not have time to extend. It lets people know how great they are by keeping others dangling.

5. Letting their dog off-leash in an on-leash area “because he’s friendly.” Leash laws were written for other people’s dogs.

4. Talking at normal volume during a movie, play, or concert, as if they were in their own living room—in a sense, they are.

3. Double-parking “for just a minute,” blocking a full lane of traffic. Hazard lights optional.

2. RSVPing yes and simply not showing up—no cancellation—to a dinner, wedding, or gathering someone paid for per head. Their presence is always a gift. Maybe next time they will bless you. Keep trying.

1. At cafes, restaurants, and bars, they say: “I’ll do the__” (matcha latte, espresso martini, avocado toast with burrata). They do not ask: “May I please have a__?” “May I please have” is a request. “I’ll do the__” is a decree. If you’re not royalty, then you’re there to serve.

A heightened sense of entitlement accompanies the fabricated self-importance, and it is a full-time job for not only many influencers but many seemingly otherwise normal adults who amuse themselves by playing status games. My observation of the egregious disregard for commonly accepted etiquette is that these people must be reincarnations of kings and queens from previous epochs, many of whom must feel that they were sent back to Earth to instruct the rest of us how to live correctly by constantly displaying their greatness in the most trivial and mundane situations.
